title: Wren and the Autopsy
premise: Oscar Marchetti, a concierge with an uncanny eye for detail, has quietly solved three deaths the police ruled accidental — and told no one. When twin letters arrive, one confessing to a fourth death and one promising more, Oscar realizes all four victims share a connection: they each once worked at the Hollowmere Hotel alongside Wren Ashby, the night auditor who vanished twenty years ago. The letters are signed 'Wren,' but Oscar suspects the real Wren is dead, and someone is using her name to punish the people who covered up her disappearance. As Oscar digs into the hotel's sealed past with help from the confessor's estranged daughter, they uncover that the beloved former owner's 'accidental' fall was murder witnessed by a teenage Wren — and the killer has been hiding in plain sight as the hotel's loyal caretaker ever since. In the end, Oscar traps the caretaker into confessing on the hotel's old intercom system, gives Wren's remains a proper burial, and finds the belonging he never had in the found family of people who finally refuse to look away.
about_author: Lior Galloway is a former night-shift receptionist at a grand old seaside hotel, where the guest ledger held more secrets than the guests did. They write mysteries about quiet observers and the families people build when their own fail them.

chapters.title: The Third Accident
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A retired judge dies in the Hollowmere's stairwell; police call it a fall, but Oscar noticed the handrail was loosened from below. Flashbacks reveal his two earlier silent investigations. He decides, again, to say nothing — until the guilt of silence curdles into resolve. Emotional beat: loneliness of the observer who helps no one by knowing everything.

chapters.title: Twin Envelopes
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Two letters arrive under his door: one confessing to the judge's murder in meticulous detail only the killer could know, the other promising 'three more before the year turns.' Both are signed Wren Ashby, a name Oscar recognizes from the hotel's oldest staff photos. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into fascination; the watcher is now watched.

chapters.title: The Girl in the Staff Photo
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, shifting to Ada Voss (the confessor's estranged daughter, who arrives demanding answers) in the final third. Ada reveals her father received the same letters before his 'heart attack' last spring. Together they pull the 2004 staff registry: Wren Ashby, night auditor, disappeared without a police report. Emotional beat: two strangers bound by letters neither understands.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Kept
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. In the basement archive, they find Wren's old ledgers with pages razored out — always the nights surrounding the founder Edmund Hollowmere's fatal fall. Oscar reconstructs the missing dates from guest receipts he memorized years ago. Someone else has been in the archive recently; cigarette ash, still warm. Emotional beat: the thrill of partnership replacing Oscar's solitary habit.

chapters.title: The Caretaker's Kindness
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Silas Brandt, the hotel's devoted caretaker for thirty years, offers help — and small kindnesses that read, on rereading, like surveillance. A second victim, the retired housekeeper Mrs. Okafor, survives a staged gas leak because Oscar breaks his own rule and warns her. Emotional beat: Oscar learns silence kills; speaking costs him his anonymity.

chapters.title: Confession, Interrupted
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada confronts her father's lawyer and learns his 'confession' was coerced — he was dying anyway, and someone traded his silence for Ada's safety. A third letter arrives naming the next target: the retired police sergeant who closed the 2004 case in one afternoon. Emotional beat: rage at how thoroughly the town protected its own.

chapters.title: Twenty Years of Small Repairs
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Following maintenance logs, Oscar maps Silas's repairs to every near-miss over two decades — each one quietly preventing discovery of what happened the night Edmund fell. They find Wren's hidden apartment above the boathouse, untouched, her final note half-written: 'He saw me see him.' Emotional beat: grief for a girl erased by everyone's convenience.

chapters.title: The Sergeant's Last Shift
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Racing a storm, they reach the sergeant's cottage too late to stop the attempt, but Oscar's warning call saves him. Cornered, Silas doesn't flee — he goes home to the Hollowmere, ascending to the roof where Edmund fell. Emotional beat: dread transmuting into clarity; the pattern completes itself.

chapters.title: Wren and the Autopsy
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, climax. On the rooftop in the rain, Silas confesses: Edmund's fall was murder to protect embezzlement, Wren witnessed it, and Silas has spent twenty years 'maintaining' the lie — including Wren's death, which he insists was an accident he couldn't admit. Oscar goads him into repeating it all through the rooftop intercom, where the sergeant and police listen below. Emotional beat: the quiet man's voice, finally loud enough.

chapters.title: A Name on the Register
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, resolution. Months later: Silas convicted, the hotel's board forced open its records, and Wren Ashby buried beneath a headstone paid for by staff past and present. Oscar, offered the manager's office, instead trains a new concierge to notice everything — and to speak. Ada stays on as archivist. Emotional beat: inheritance reclaimed; belonging chosen, not assigned.
